9. Running the Game#

This chapter is for the GM. Everything a player needs is in chapters 1–8.

Your Job#

  1. Describe Halcyon vividly and briefly: smell, sound, one weird detail.
  2. Ask questions and use the answers. "Vex, which gang tattooed you?"
  3. Call for rolls only when failure is interesting. Otherwise say yes.
  4. Make failures move the story: fail, succeed at a cost, or things get worse. Never "nothing happens."
  5. Hand out Juice generously; roughly one per player per session, more for great moments.

Setting DCs#

Pick the DC from the Core Rules table: 13 when unsure. Add advantage or disadvantage for circumstances instead of fiddling with numbers. If an enemy is opposing the check directly, use its TN.

Running the Enemy Phase#

  • Declare all enemy actions at once: "The two Cleaners fire at Vex and Juno; the Drain Beast grabs Ozzie."
  • Players roll their defenses; you just read out Damage and riders.
  • Mooks and Soldiers act simply. Elites and Bosses should feel smart: focus the weak, punish clumping, flee when beaten.
  • Spread attacks unless the fiction says otherwise. Focusing one player every round is how you get a death in a Standard fight.
  • Let the fiction override the grid: a Brute can smash a wall, a Skirmisher can jump down a stairwell.
  • Area attacks catch whoever is inside. Be honest about positions. Heavies (big Area, Engulf) are built to punish a bunched-up party; tell players that spreading out is the counter, and don't line them up in a corridor for the Heavy unless they walked into it.
  • Packs focus. Pack, Flanker and Overwhelm creatures gang up on one freelancer; that's their whole point. Everyone else should still spread attacks.
  • Default tactics (what the arcade's enemies do, and a good baseline for yours):
    • Area attackers aim where they catch the most freelancers and the fewest friends; Bulky ones won't fire into their own allies.
    • Melee enemies close in and flank; ranged enemies stay out of melee reach and shoot.
    • Anything with no target in reach Dashes toward one.
    • Elites, Bosses and Hunters go for the freelancer with the lowest HP about half the time; everyone else picks a target that makes sense in the fiction.
    • A Taunted enemy goes for its taunter if it can.
    • Bosses use their Interrupt on the first good opening each round and summon when their minions are thin.

Missions#

GRAFT contracts follow a simple shape. Each is about one session.

  1. Brief. A GRAFT handler explains the job and the pay. Players ask questions, buy gear.
  2. Approach. Getting in: travel, a social obstacle, or a skill challenge.
  3. Trouble. One or two fights or hazards. Something is not what the brief said.
  4. Heart. The objective: a boss, a choice, a sample, a person.
  5. Out. Escape, consequences, a Breather if earned.
  6. Debrief. Get paid, level up, downtime.

The Spill Clock#

Give each mission a 6-segment clock. Tick it when players dawdle, make noise, Overload, or fail a roll badly. When it fills, the situation escalates: reinforcements, a flood, a Cleaner squad, the building collapses. Then reset it. Show it to the players; it makes them hurry.

Skill Challenges#

For a chase, a hack, or a climb, ask for 3 successes before 3 failures (Standard DC). Each player says how they help and picks a stat. Each failure costs something: HP (T-level Damage), a tick on the Spill Clock, or lost gear.

Downtime (between missions)#

Each freelancer picks one:

  • Clinic: install your new node, splice a Sample, remove a Scar or Fault, or (at levels 4 and 7) go through a supervised Chrysalis.
  • Side Gig: earn 50 × level Scrip.
  • Dig: learn a secret about the next mission (the GM answers one question truthfully).
  • Rest: clear all Injuries and gain 1 Juice at the start of next session.
  • Bond: spend time with a contact; they'll do you a favour on the next mission.

Evolution at the Table#

Evolutions (levels 4 and 7) are the biggest moments in a freelancer's life. Make them land.

  • Seed it. In the mission before, describe symptoms: an itch under the plating, a second heartbeat, a voice in the wiring, clothes that don't fit.
  • Chrysalis (optional downtime scene). At the debrief where someone reaches level 4 or 7, play one short scene of the change starting: a cocoon in a flooded basement (Bio), or an emergency overhaul on a clinic table while GRAFT techs argue (Chrome). Ask the player one question: "What do you lose?" (a face, a voice, a fear, a friend's trust). Write it down; it's a hook.
  • Emergence. In the next mission's first fight, the player Emerges at the start of their first turn (chapter 2A): temporary HP, nearby enemies Shaken, a free Signature Surge. Give them the spotlight. Describe enemies backing away.
  • Let them win big once. The first mission after an Evolution should feel like a victory lap. Then raise the stakes (see below).
  • Different speeds. Everyone Evolves at the same level, so the whole party spikes together. Lean into it: the Spill Clock, GRAFT and the factions all notice evolved freelancers.

Difficulty Across the Campaign#

Every enemy has a Boss Rating (one of it is a fair fight for 4 level-N freelancers) and a Minion Rating (four of it are). Build fights with the unit budget in Threats: one unit per freelancer is a Hard (fair) fight, ×½ Easy, ×¾ Standard, ×1¼ Deadly. The ratings already account for each level, including the Evolutions, so the same budget works from level 1 to 10.

What the Evolutions change is last stage's monsters. A creature rated in the previous stage falls apart against freshly Evolved freelancers (four MR 3 creatures: Hard at level 3, Easy at level 4), and one rated in the next stage is twice as dangerous as its number suggests.

Party levelPlanWhat to do
1–3 (Base)Standard fights, one Hard per missionDowns happen; Rats and Pickers teach Pack tactics, the Drain Beast and Boiler Hulk teach spreading out
4 (just Evolved)A victory lapBring back level-3 enemies (they're Easy now), then one Hard fight with Evolution I creatures so the new body has something to push against
5–6Hard set piecesMix a Heavy centrepiece with a Pack; add Purgers and enemies that hit weak defenses (Resist for Sirens, Endure for Oracles)
7 (Evolved again)A victory lap with bigger monstersLevel-6 enemies are Easy now; open with them, then show a Feral Evolved or a Gutter Leviathan
8–10Hard and Deadly fights; the finale should be DeadlyBosses whose Shift lands after Final Form is spent; Seraph Gunships over open ground

Between Breathers: a fully rested party can take about one Hard fight plus one Standard fight, or three Standard fights, before it needs one (an estimate from HP lost per fight; the sims only test fully rested parties). The ratings assume full HP and Flux 0, so a tired party should face less.

Checks don't scale. A DC 16 door stays DC 16. At high level, threaten what Forms are bad at (ask the Juggernaut for a Gumption check, the Oracle to win an arm-wrestle), and put Extreme (19), Mutant (22), Monstrous (25) and Mythic (28) obstacles in the way. A level 7 primary stat of +8 makes Hard checks routine; that's the point of Evolving.

Rewards#

  • Levels: one per mission (Advancement).
  • Scrip: 200 + (100 × mission level) each, plus bonuses for style or recovered Samples.
  • Samples: from Bosses and some Elites.
  • Juice: in the moment.

Factions at a Glance#

Ostrander RemnantErase evidence, retake the citySilence, stolen SamplesProof of what caused the Spill

d6ClientJobLocationTwist

Pacing Guidelines#

  • Fights: 2–3 per mission. One should be Hard. The boss can be Deadly if the players found a way to soften it. Size every fight with the encounter budget, and scale Bosses for party size (Threats §6).
  • Breathers: let the party take them, but make the clock tick.
  • Surges: encourage them. If a player never Unleashes, ask what their body is doing. Surges are the fun.
  • Overload: describe it gleefully, never as a punishment. It's the setting coming through the character.

Safety#

Body horror can hit hard. Before play, agree as a table what's off-limits (lines) and what should happen off-screen (veils). Anyone can pause a scene, no questions asked.

Rulings Log#

Keep a list of rulings at the table. If one should become a rule, add it to Current_Work.md as an open question.

10. Threats#

Every enemy is built from three parts: Threat level (T), Role and Traits. Every enemy also carries two ratings that tell you how to use it: a Boss Rating and a Minion Rating. You can build a new enemy in a few minutes, or read one off the roster below.

1. Ratings: BR and MR#

  • Boss Rating (BR N): one of this creature, alone, is a fair fight for 4 fully rested level-N freelancers.
  • Minion Rating (MR N): four of this creature are a fair fight for 4 fully rested level-N freelancers.

A fair fight means, for a fully rested party (full HP, Flux 0, kit full):

MeasureFair bandTypical at the rating
Party wins90%+93–99%
At least one freelancer goes Down40–60% (50% target)40–55% (Bosses 25–35%: their fights are long, so death risk sets the rating)
Anyone dies5% or less0–5%
Rounds3–72–6
Party HP lost25–50%30–45%

A creature's rating is the lowest party level at which its fight stays inside all of the first three limits. Ratings come from simulated fights with real builder characters of every Form (tools/encounter_sim.py, 1,000 fights per level; see Current_Work.md, Enemy Calibration). <1 means it is never a fair fight in that use even at level 1 (one Spill Rat). 10+ means no level-10 party can take it in that use (four Feral Evolved).

Read the gap. MR − BR says how a creature wants to be used:

  • About 3 (Generalists): fine alone at its BR or in a group at its MR.
  • 2 or less: Heavies. Big Area attacks make them deadly alone, and especially against big or bunched-up parties; in a crowd they get in each other's way (Bulky, Friendly fire, Interference, Territorial). Use one as a centrepiece.
  • 4 or more: Packs. Pack, Flanker, Overwhelm, Crowd, Linked and Frenzy only work with friends. One is a speed bump; four are a fight.

2. Threat Level#

T runs 1–10. It sets the numbers; the ratings tell you who it's for.

TGuardTNHPDamageBonus
1121328102
2131330112
3141438163
4141662255
5151774296
6161878306
71720150469
81821158479
919221624810
1020231685010

Beyond T10: +1 Guard, +1 TN, +8 HP and +4 Damage per T. Round role multipliers to the nearest whole number.

  • Guard is what players attack against. TN is the Attack DC players defend against, and the DC for checks that oppose the creature directly (Taunt, Analyze, Puppet).
  • Damage is fixed, no rolling. Area attacks deal it to everyone caught who fails (half to those who succeed). Bonus is the unit for Traits (about ⅕ of Damage).
  • Why the jumps at T4 and T7? Freelancers Evolve at levels 4 and 7 and roughly double in power. The table jumps with them, so a T-N Soldier stays a fair fight at level N. The Evolution still lands hard: last stage's monsters fall apart (four MR 3 creatures, a Hard fight at level 3, are an Easy fight at level 4).
  • Hits are big. A failed defense against a same-T Soldier costs about ⅔ of an average freelancer's HP. Defenses succeed about half the time, Brace and cover matter, and healing between hits matters more.

4. Traits#

Pick 1–3. ΔBR / ΔMR is how much each Trait moves the ratings (measured; ½ = half a rating step). Traits marked 0 / 0 change how a fight feels (Flux, Surges, positioning) more than how dangerous it is.

Every Heavy needs at least one horde penalty (Bulky, Interference or Territorial). Without one, four Heavies are a massacre (MR +4).

Who's caught by an Area? Whoever is inside it. The ratings assume a party of 4 that isn't trying to bunch up or spread out: a 10-ft area catches the target and about 1 in 3 of the others, 20 ft about 1 in 2, 30 ft about 2 in 3, and each freelancer beyond four adds ~8% to those odds. On a battle map Heavies catch more (about 3¼ of 4 freelancers per Area in the arcade's grid fights, even with the party spreading out), so on a grid a Heavy costs ×1¼ units (§5). If your table fights shoulder to shoulder in corridors, Heavies hit harder than their rating; tell players that spreading out is the counter.

The ½-step values for Mimic, Hunter and Shielded are T5-only and rounded down; Territorial and Damage Gate weren't measured on their own (— / about).

Building a new enemy: pick T and Role, read its typical BR/MR, add the Traits' ΔBR/ΔMR, and round. That's within about one step of what the simulator says. If you want it exact, add it to tools/encounter_roster.py and run python3 tools/encounter_sim.py rate "Name".

5. Building an Encounter#

1. Budget. A Hard (fair) fight is worth one unit per freelancer, with a small correction for very small and very large groups:

Freelancers23456
Hard budget (units)1¾2¾45½7

2. Difficulty. Multiply the budget:

DifficultyBudgetWhat it costs a fully rested party of 4 (sims)
Easy×½~10% HP; Downs rare (3–6%)
Standard×¾~20% HP; someone goes Down in ~1 fight in 5
Hard×1 (fair)~30–40% HP; someone goes Down about half the time; deaths rare
Deadly×1¼~50–60% HP; Downs likely; 10–25% chance the party loses or someone dies
Overwhelming×1½+The party loses about half the time. Don't, unless running is an option

3. Spend it. A creature's units depend on how far its rating is from the party level:

Rating − party level−3−2−10+1+2+3
In a group (use MR)⅓½¾11½23
As a centrepiece (use BR)1½2346811

Value at most one creature per encounter by BR (the centrepiece); everything else uses MR. A centrepiece Boss already scaled for the party (§6) is worth the whole Hard budget.

4. Check the stage and the map. Freelancers double in power at each Evolution, so ratings don't carry across one:

  • A creature rated in the party's next stage (e.g. MR 4 against level 3) counts double its units. Avoid more than one.
  • A creature rated in the party's previous stage (e.g. MR 3 against level 4) counts as one step lower than the table says.
  • Playing on a grid? Count each Heavy at ×1¼ its units. Everything else costs the same on a map as off it (the evidence is in §7).

Worked example. Four level-5 freelancers, Hard fight, budget 4: a Glasshide as the centrepiece (BR 5 → 4 units) is the whole fight. Or a Bloom Knight (MR 5 → 1) + two Stitchwork Brood (MR 6 → 1½ each) = 4. For a Standard fight (3 units), take 3 Cleaner Hounds (MR 5 → 1 each).

6. Party Size#

Use the budget table above, plus three adjustments the sims found:

  • Bosses: HP ×1 per freelancer and Damage × (freelancers ÷ 4), summoned creatures' Damage too. With 3 freelancers: ×¾; with 5: ×1¼. Without this, a Boss fair for 4 is a near-TPK for 3 (Matriarch: 77% win, 16% death) and a walkover for 5 (13% Down).
  • Heavies vs 5+ freelancers count ×1½ units. More bodies means more of them inside every Area, and Engulf punishes it: against 5 a Heavy's ratings drop only ~½–¾, other creatures' drop ~1.
  • Quick shift: if you'd rather move ratings than budgets, a creature's BR and MR are about +1 against 3 freelancers, −1 against 5 (+2 / −1½ for 2 / 6). Heavies: +1 / −½ to −¾ (as minions vs 3: only +½).

7. At the Table#

  • From Evolution II, lone big targets melt. Four L7 freelancers can deal 150+ damage a round. Elites and Bosses rated for them already account for that, but anything rated in the previous stage dies before it acts. Use the stage rule above.
  • Heavies want room; Packs want company. Put a Heavy in an open hall with the party bunched at a chokepoint and it lives up to its BR. Put four Rats on one freelancer and they live up to their MR.
  • Final Form (level 10) turns one fight per Lockdown into a rout. The ratings assume it's off. Save the finale's real threat for the Boss's Shift.
  • On a battle map the budgets hold, except for Heavies. Book-budget Hard fights played on a grid in the arcade engine (1,200 fights for a party of 4, all levels, tools/grid_budget.js) stayed fair: 94% won, someone Down in 31%, a death in 4%, 4 rounds. Fights with a Heavy ran hot: a death in 7% and someone Down in 39%, because a Heavy's Area caught 3¼ of 4 freelancers on average against the 2½–3 the ratings assume. With Heavy fights cut to ×0.8 they matched the rest (death 2%, Down 30%), hence the ×1¼ units for Heavies on a grid in §5. See Positioning. (The arcade's own difficulty factors are a video-game setting, not a tabletop rule: see the Arcade vs Tabletop appendix.)
  • Terrain, objectives ("hold the pump for 3 rounds"), and fleeing enemies matter more than numbers. Use them.

11. Starter Mission — Pumpstation 9#

A one-session mission for 3–5 level 1 freelancers. Five pregenerated characters (one per Base Form) are at the end. Numbers assume 4 players; each fight lists what to change for 3 or 5 (checked in tools/sim_results/11_starter_mission.md).

The Brief#

Handler Dez Okafor, GRAFT Field Office 3, over a crackling radio:

"Pumpstation 9 keeps the Fenwick Ward from flooding. Since Tuesday it's been pumping Mutagen into their water instead of out. Ward council's paying us; we're paying you. 300 Scrip each to shut the intake and kill whatever's in there. Bring back anything weird. Don't drink anything."

What's really going on: A Scrapjack crew, paid by an Ostrander Remnant agent, planted a Brood Matriarch egg in the intake to test whether a mutagenic bloom can be weaponized through a water supply. The Matriarch has rooted into the pipes. The Scrapjacks are still here, stripping the pump room and waiting for their pickup.

Spill Clock: 6 segments. Tick it for loud noises, long rests, failed stealth, and Overloads. When it fills, see Out.

Scene 1: The Fenwick Toll#

The only dry road to the pumpstation crosses a Ward barricade. Three Ward Toughs (T1 Soldiers, MR 1) want a 50-Scrip "toll" each.

  • Talk: Chutzpah DC 13 lets the party through free; with a good argument ("we're here to fix your water") roll with advantage.
  • Fight (Standard, 3 units): 3 Ward Toughs (MR 1 → 1 unit each). For 3 players use 2; for 5 use 4. They're Cowardly (they surrender at half HP), and the Ward council will dock the party's pay by 100.
  • Sneak: A group Moxie check DC 13 through the flooded alleys. Failure ticks the clock and they arrive soaked (each takes 2 damage from the cold).
  • Clue: Any Tough knows "some chrome-heads went in Monday with a crate."

Scene 2: The Pump Hall#

A three-storey hall of rusting turbines, waist-deep green water on the lower floor, catwalks above. A Scrapjack Picker is prying copper from the turbines while two Spill Rats nest in the pipes. More Pickers are asleep upstairs (a second one joins if the Spill Clock ticks during the fight).

  • Fight (Standard, 3 units): 1 Picker (MR 2 → 1½) + 2 Spill Rats (MR 1 → 1 each). For 3 players: 1 Picker + 1 Rat. For 5: the same fight (Packs focus one target, so a bigger party doesn't make Downs much rarer: 26% with 5 players vs 27% with 4); add a third Rat only for a Hard fight. The Rats attack anyone in the water first, all on the same freelancer (Pack, Overwhelm). v0.2's 2 Pickers + 4 Rats is a Deadly 7 units under the new table: an 82% chance someone goes Down.
  • Terrain: Water is difficult terrain. Catwalks give partial cover. A turbine can be restarted (Gumption DC 13, Action): everyone in the water takes 7 Shock (Area, Endure for half).
  • Twist: A Picker carries an Ostrander-coded data chit and a radio: their pickup is "in one hour." Reading the chit (Gumption DC 16 or a Hack deck) reveals the plan.
  • If a Picker is captured: Chutzpah DC 13 to make them talk. They know the egg went "into the big intake pipe."

Breather: The control room is defensible. The party can take a Breather here (tick the clock twice).

Scene 3: The Intake#

A flooded concrete cathedral where the river pipe meets the pumps. Glowing roots of flesh cover the walls. In the middle, fused to the intake grate, is the Brood Matriarch with two Spill Rats already crawling on her.

  • Fight (Hard): the Matriarch alone (BR 1, a whole Hard budget); she Births her own Brood Spawn. Scale her for the party (Threats §6): HP and all Damage ×¾ for 3 players (HP 43), ×1¼ for 5 (HP 72). The two Spill Rats on her flee into the pipes when the fight starts. See Threats.
  • The Valve: A huge manual valve stands 20 ft from the Matriarch. Three successful Grit or Gumption checks (DC 13, Action each) close it. When it closes, she shrieks, is Dazed until the end of the next Enemy Phase, and can't Birth for the rest of the fight. Closing the valve also completes the mission objective, even if she survives.
  • The Sample: Harvest with Gumption DC 12 after she dies: Brood Web (Burst + Snare).

Out#

  • If the clock filled at any point, two Ostrander Cleaners (T3 Soldiers, MR 3 → 2 units each: Standard-to-Hard at level 1 by the sims, Deadly for a tired party) arrive by boat as the party leaves. Running is the smart choice: a group Moxie check DC 13 to reach the alleys. On failure, the Cleaners get one Enemy Phase of shots before the party escapes.
  • If the clock never filled, the pickup boat arrives empty; the party can ambush it and capture the Ostrander agent, Mr. Hale, a calm man with no mutations and an expensive umbrella.

Debrief#

  • Pay: 300 Scrip each; +100 each for the data chit or Mr. Hale; −100 total if they fought the Ward.
  • GRAFT asks for the Sample. Players who hand it over get +50 each. Players who keep it can splice it.
  • Everyone reaches level 2.
  • Hook: the data chit lists five more pumpstations.

  • Surges: 1 Field Dressing (Infuse + Mend: 2d8+3 HP) · 2 Acid Bloom (Burst + Corrode, Gumption: +4, 2d6, Exposed) · 3 Stomp (Pulse + Quake: +3, 2d6, Prone) · 4 Wild
  • Gear: Medic kit (Pistol, Standard melee, 2 Medkits, 2 Stims)
  • Perk: Patch heals +1 extra; Scars and Faults cost him half to remove. Stim Gland twice per Breather; can't be Poisoned. Splice: Knit 2, roll both Overload tables and choose, Upkeep 25 (prepaid).

Rook — Juggernaut (Chrome)#

Ward militia veteran with piston fists, a riveted hide and a voice like a closing door.

  • Stats: Grit +3, Nerve +2, Chutzpah +1, Moxie +0, Gumption −1
  • HP 20 · Armor 2 · Speed 30 · Flux Limit 7
  • Defenses: Dodge +1, Endure +4, Resist +3
  • Knacks: Squad Tactics, Intimidation, Demolition
  • Augments: Hide: Plating, Thick, Barbs · Limbs: Natural Weapons, Extra Arm · Glands: Spit (all Chrome)
  • Attacks: Sledge +4, 1d10+3 · Piston Fists +4, 1d8+3 (+1 die once per turn, Extra Arm) · Spit +3 (Nerve), 1d8+2
  • Surges: 1 Piston Slam (Strike + Kinetic: +4, 3d10+3, push 10 ft) · 2 Floor Breaker (Pulse + Quake: +4, 2d6, Prone) · 3 Bulkhead (Infuse + Shell: 2d6+3 temp HP, +1 Armor) · 4 Wild
  • Gear: Bruiser kit (Heavy melee, Medkit, Grapnel)
  • Perk: +2 to his roll in group initiative; Brace as a Quick action once per combat. Melee attackers that damage him take 2. Chrome: Firmware, Glitch table, disadvantage vs Shock, Upkeep 75 (GRAFT prepays 25).

Mags — Siren (Bio)#

A Bloom street-preacher with a voice that harmonises with itself and a crowd that follows her home.

  • Stats: Chutzpah +3, Moxie +2, Gumption +1, Grit +0, Nerve −1
  • HP 12 · Armor 1 · Speed 40 · Flux Limit 4
  • Defenses: Dodge +3, Endure +1, Resist +0 (advantage: Iron Will)

  • Gear: Face kit (Concealed Pistol, Light melee, Hack deck, Flashbang, +50 Scrip)
  • Perk: Once per Lockdown, reroll an Overload result and choose. Rally as a Quick action. Can't be Shaken. Bio: Knit 3, Bloom table. Her Limit is only 4: she will Overload. That's the point of her.

12. Quick Reference#

The Roll#

d20 + Stat (+ Rank) ≥ target. Rank always on attacks and defenses; on checks only with a Knack. Ties: player wins.
Rank = level ÷ 2, round up (1–5). Adv/Dis: 2d20 keep high/low. Nat 20 attack = Crit (double dice). Nat 20 defense = no damage + attacker Exposed. Nat 1 = fail.

DC10 Easy13 Standard16 Hard19 Extreme22 Mutant25 Monstrous28 Mythic

Stages: Base +3/+2/+1/+0/−1 → Evo I (L4) +5/+3/+2/+1/+0 → Evo II (L7) +8/+4/+3/+2/+1 → Final Form (L10, active) primary +10. Each Evolution: stats, +1 Prime, die jump (d6→d8→d12), +1 Signature Surge, Evolution node, new look; Emerge in the next first fight (temp HP 2×level, enemies within 30 ft Shaken, first Signature free).
Nodes: L1 = 3 primary + 2 secondary + 1 tertiary. Each level: +1 primary (auto) + 1 secondary or tertiary. Tier II: L4+ & 3 nodes in tree. Apex: L7+ & 6 other nodes, primary/secondary only. Primary full at L8 → overflow.

Stats#

Grit smash/endure/HP · Moxie dodge/sneak/finesse · Nerve aim/notice/resist/Limit · Gumption fix/hack/heal/know · Chutzpah talk/lie/taunt/rally/Dread
Defenses: Dodge = Moxie+Rank · Endure = Grit+Rank · Resist = Nerve+Rank

Derived#

HP 12 + 2×Grit, +5/level · Flux Limit 4 + Rank + Nerve (Splice −1) · Speed 30 · Armor max 4 (Unbreakable 5, Siege Hide 6) · Juice start 1, max 3

Round#

Player Phase (any order) → Enemy Phase (all at once, players defend).
Turn: Move + Action + Quick; 1 Reaction per round.
Actions: Attack · Unleash · Dash · Brace · Help · Patch · Analyze · Taunt · Rally · Grapple/Shove · Other
Quick: draw, stim, Churn, Target Lock, talk
Reactions: Opportunity Strike when an enemy leaves your reach (melee weapon attack); each enemy gets one per round on you if you leave its reach (move carefully, at half speed, to avoid it). Dazed: no Reactions.
Ranges: Help 30 ft · Analyze/Taunt/Rally 60 ft · Patch touch · ranged weapons to 2× range at disadvantage (not Areas/grenades) · enemy adjacent to a shooter = disadvantage.
Positioning: theatre of the mind (Close 5 ft · Near 30 ft · Far 120 ft · Distant) or grid (1 square = 5 ft, diagonals = 1; 30 ft = 6 squares; 10-ft burst = 5×5 squares; 15-ft cone 3 deep; line 1 wide; walls block sight and Areas).
Wait: go later in the Player Phase if you haven't acted. Boss Interrupt: one action (no Move) after any player's turn, once per round.
Damage: Rank × weapon die + stat. Armor −X per hit (min 1). Area: miss/successful defense = half.

Surges#

Prime at combat start: roll Sequence die × Prime (2; 3 from L4; 4 from L7). Doubles = Amped (0 Flux). Wild slot = roll Wild table (each separately, never doubles).
Unleash (Action): pay 1 Flux + 1 per Twist; a missed Strike/Bolt stays Primed. Churn (Quick): +1 Flux, roll once more; not on a turn you Unleash (max Prime + 1 held).
Signature Surges (1 from L4, 2 from L7): always Primed, once per round each, normal Flux, not on the Sequence.
Surge stat: the Shape's stat or the stat of the Effect's tree (Hide Grit · Limbs Grit/Moxie · Senses Nerve · Glands Gumption · Wiring Moxie · Mind Chutzpah).
Juice: reroll a d20 · choose a Prime · end a condition.

Flux & Overload#

Gain Flux: Unleash, Churn, Push. Over Limit → Overload: take Rank d6 (min 1 HP left), roll d12 Bloom (Bio) / Glitch (Chrome) / both, pick (Splice), Flux → 0. Breather/Lockdown → Flux 0. Last Gasp: once per Lockdown, at 0 HP Overload instead and stay at 1 HP.

Conditions (until end of affected creature's next turn)#

Blinded dis. on attacks, attackers adv. · Burning 2×source Rank dmg at the start of its next turn, then out · Dazed no Quick/Reaction/Specials; Boss 1 action · Exposed −2 Guard / −2 defense · Held speed 0 · Poisoned half damage dealt · Prone melee adv./ranged dis. against; stand = ½ speed · Shaken dis. on attacks & checks, can't approach source · Veiled adv. on defense & next attack
Enemy advantage = player rolls defense with disadvantage.

Down#

0 HP: Prone, crawl 5 ft. End of each Enemy Phase: Endure DC 10, fail = Death mark (nat 20: up at 1 HP). Damage while Down = mark (2 on a failed defense vs a Boss). 3 marks = dead. Any healing = up. Roll Injury (d6). Everyone Down = the fight is lost. Bosses end one condition at the start of their turn.

Rest#

Breather (1 hr, 2 per Lockdown): regain ½ Max HP (+Knit, which also triggers after each combat), Flux 0, clear Death marks. Lockdown (8 hr safe): full reset.

13. Character Building Guide#

This chapter walks you from a blank sheet to a finished level 1 freelancer, then through both Evolutions to level 10. It tells you what to pick and in what order. The rules themselves live in chapters 1–8; when they disagree with this guide, they win.

Prefer clicking? The Character Builder (online) follows these steps, places your picks, checks legality, Evolves you at 4 and 7, and prints a sheet.

Level 1, Step by Step#

1. Concept#

One sentence with a job, a body change, and a flaw: "Ex-Ward electrician who wired her voice into the power grid and can't stop broadcasting."

2. Base Form#

Pick the Form that matches what you want to do in a fight:

You want to...FormPrimary statTrees (primary / secondary / tertiary)
Hold the line, protect, hit hard up closeJuggernautGritHide / Limbs / Glands
Be fast, slippery and deadly in meleeSkitterMoxieWiring / Limbs / Senses
Shoot, spot, and bend luckOracleNerveSenses / Mind / Wiring
Heal, poison, out-thinkAlembicGumptionGlands / Hide / Mind
Talk, Taunt, control, leadSirenChutzpahMind / Wiring / Limbs

3. Stats#

Your Form sets +3 / +2 / +1. Put +0 and −1 in the two stats left over. Pick the −1 for the stat you'll be tested on least. A −1 in Grit costs 2 HP and a weak Endure; a −1 in Moxie means a weak Dodge (the most common defense); a −1 in Nerve means a weak Resist and a lower Flux Limit.

4. Origin#

Roll d6 or choose. Write its Knack and Perk. Perks with numbers: Corporate Washout +100 Scrip; Lab Escapee +1 Surge known; Clinic Rat +Rank to Patch; Ward Militia +2 on group initiative.

5. Knacks#

Your Origin gives one; write two more (3 total). Narrow and concrete: Sewer Routes, not Survival. You gain one more at levels 3, 6 and 9.

6. Augments#

Take 6 nodes, only from your Form's trees:

TreeNodes at level 1
PrimaryRoot + 2 Tier I
SecondaryRoot + 1 Tier I
TertiaryRoot

For each tree, choose its Material (Bio or Chrome) when you take the Root:

You haveYou arePerkCost
Only Bio treesBioKnit: +Rank HP per Bio tree after each fight and BreatherBloom table
Only Chrome treesChromeFirmware: swap one Primed Surge per fightGlitch table, disadvantage vs Shock, 25 Scrip Upkeep per Chrome tree per mission
BothSpliceKnit (counting Bio trees) + Firmware (Chrome-tree parts) + roll both Overload tables, choose oneChrome's costs above, Flux Limit −1

What each Root unlocks (your Surge parts, fixed by your Form): Hide → Pulse, Quake, Shell · Limbs → Wave, Snare · Senses → Glare, Veil · Glands → Burst, Toxin, Corrode, Mend · Wiring → Shock, Blaze, Haste · Mind → Dread, Link.

Three Roots give you a weapon-like attack: Natural Weapons (Limbs, d8 melee, Grit/Moxie), Spit (Glands, d8, 30 ft, Nerve/Gumption) and Mind Spike (Mind, d8, 60 ft, Nerve/Chutzpah).

7. Surges and the Sequence#

Build 3 Surges (4 for a Lab Escapee) and write them in Sequence slots 1–3. Your Sequence die is d4, so slot 4 is Wild (a Lab Escapee fills it). Prime is 2.

The Surge recipe:

  1. Shape: any base Shape (Strike, Bolt, Infuse) or one your Roots unlocked.
  2. Effect: a damage Effect (base: Kinetic) for Strike/Bolt/Burst/Wave/Pulse, or an Infuse Effect for Infuse. Never mix. Every Form has at least two Infuse Effects.
  3. Attack stat: the Shape's stat or the stat of the tree that unlocked the Effect (Hide Grit · Limbs Grit/Moxie · Senses Nerve · Glands Gumption · Wiring Moxie · Mind Chutzpah). This is how every Form attacks with its primary stat.
  4. Twist (optional): one at Rank 1–2, two different from Rank 3. Each must match the Shape (Chain: Strike/Bolt; Linger: area Shapes; Leech, Overcharge: damage only; Sure, Reach, Hush: any).
  5. Cost: 1 Flux + 1 per Twist.
  6. Name it and describe it in your Form's look.

Numbers on a Surge:

ShapeAttackDamage
Strike (melee)Grit or Moxie (or Effect's tree stat) + Rank(Rank+1)d10 + stat
Bolt (60 ft)Nerve (or Effect's tree stat) + Rank(Rank+1)d8 + stat
Burst (10-ft radius, 60 ft)Nerve (or Effect's tree stat) + Rank(Rank+1)d6, no stat
Wave (15-ft cone / 30-ft line)Grit or Nerve (or Effect's tree stat) + Rank(Rank+1)d6, no stat
Pulse (10 ft around you)Grit (or Effect's tree stat) + Rank(Rank+1)d6, no stat
Infuse (you or an ally, 30 ft)no rollper Effect

Add +1 die for Kinetic and +2 dice for Overcharge. Burst and Wave hit allies in the area too.

A good first three: one reliable damage Surge in your primary stat, one control Surge (a rider that fits your trees), and one Infuse or area Surge for the team. Think ahead: at level 4 one Surge becomes your always-ready Signature, so the one you'd want every round is a good candidate.

8. Gear and Scrip#

Take one Starting Kit (Ch 8). All include Light armor (Armor 1), GRAFT ID, radio, flashlight, 2 rations and 1 Damper. Then take 50 Scrip (+100 Corporate Washout, +50 Face kit) and buy from Gear if you like.

  • Weapons: Damage = Rank × die + stat; one Mod per weapon (100 Scrip). Natural Weapons can take a Mod; Spit and Mind Spike can't.
  • You wear one armor (Light or Heavy), plus an optional Shield. Armor max 4 (5 with Unbreakable, 6 for a Juggernaut with Siege Hide).
  • Upkeep: 25 Scrip per Chrome tree (and per Smart-Link) each mission. GRAFT prepays 25 of your first mission's.

10. Trackers#

Mark the boxes you'll use in play: Flux (up to your Limit; going over is an Overload), Death marks (3), Breathers (2 per Lockdown), Last Gasp (1 per Lockdown), Juice (start each session with 1). Later: Signature Surges and Final Form (1 per Lockdown).

11. Drive#

Answer: Why did you take the Mutagen? What do you want before the campaign ends? Who in Halcyon do you owe, or hate? Give the GM at least one name.

Leveling Up (1–10)#

One mission = one level (Ch 7). Each level, in order:

  1. +5 Max HP (+2 more with Thick).
  2. +1 primary-tree node (always; you choose which) and +1 node in your secondary or tertiary tree. Gates: Tier II needs level 4 + 3 nodes in the tree; an Apex needs level 7 + 6 other nodes in the tree, and only in your primary or secondary tree. From level 9 the primary pick overflows into secondary/tertiary.
  3. +1 Surge into the next empty slot. You may also rewrite one Surge, or rebuild one Signature.
  4. Optional respec: swap one node for another of the same pick type that you qualify for.
  5. At levels 4 and 7, Evolve (checklist below).
  6. Recalculate Rank, HP, defenses, Limit, weapon dice.

The Evolution Checklist (levels 4 and 7)#

  1. Stats: Evo I → +5 / +3 / +2 / +1 / +0. Evo II → +8 / +4 / +3 / +2 / +1 (same order as your level 1 placement).
  2. Recalculate HP (Grit changed), defenses, Flux Limit (Nerve changed), and every attack and Surge line.
  3. Prime +1 (3, then 4). Sequence die up (d8, then d12): you'll have new Wild slots.
  4. Write your Form's Evolution node into your primary tree (Ch 3).
  5. Build a Signature Surge and write it in a Signature box. It's always Primed; once per round; normal Flux.
  6. Describe your new look (your Form's stage table in Ch 2A), and plan your Emergence with the GM.

Final Form (level 10): once per Lockdown at the start of a combat: primary stat +2, Prime two extra, every Surge Amped.

  • Lab Escapee has one fewer Wild slot (none at levels 6 and 10). It never adds Signatures.
  • In play you may also gain: Scars/Faults from Overloads (some change numbers: Hollow Bones, Drained Cell, Brittle Shell, Sticky Relay), a Blossom Knack, Patch Applied (+1 Limit), Injuries until Lockdown, and Samples (a Surge spliced into a Wild slot for 100 Scrip; it may use the Boss's parts).
  • Scrip: each mission pays 200 + 100 × level; pay Upkeep before the next one.

Planning tip: your primary tree fills by level 8 whatever you do, so the real choices are order (what you want before Evolution I) and where your secondary/tertiary picks go. Pour them into the secondary if you want its Apex at level 7–9 (you'll need 7 nodes there), or spread them for utility.

Common Mistakes#

  • Taking a node outside your Form's trees. You only have three.
  • Wrong split at level 1. It's 3 primary / 2 secondary / 1 tertiary, Roots first.
  • Skipping the primary pick. You get one every level until the tree is full (level 8), and must take it.
  • Tier II before level 4, or with fewer than 3 nodes in that tree.
  • An Apex in your tertiary tree, before level 7, or with fewer than 6 other nodes in the tree.
  • Choosing your Evolution node. It's fixed by your Form and comes free at 4 and 7.
  • Forgetting to recalculate at an Evolution: HP (Grit), Limit (Nerve), every attack and Surge line.
  • Writing a Signature on your Sequence. It goes in its own box and doesn't count toward Surges known.
  • Using a part you haven't unlocked. Only base parts (Strike, Bolt, Infuse, Kinetic) and your Roots' unlocks.
  • Infuse with a damage Effect, or Bolt with Mend. Infuse only takes Infuse Effects.
  • Wrong Twist: Chain on a Burst, Linger on a Bolt, Overcharge on Infuse, two Twists before Rank 3, the same Twist twice.
  • Adding the stat to area damage. Burst, Wave and Pulse roll dice only.
  • Forgetting Splice −1 Limit or Chrome Upkeep (and disadvantage vs Shock).
  • Armor over the cap, or wearing Light and Heavy together.
  • Knowing too many Surges. Surges known = level + 2 (Lab Escapee +1, Samples extra); the rest are Wild, on purpose.

Worked Example: Dree "Brownout" Ocampo (Siren)#

Level 1 — Siren#

  1. Concept: Ex-Ward electrician who wired her voice into the power grid. She's a pirate-radio preacher of the blackout who can't stop broadcasting.
  2. Form: Siren (Chutzpah primary; Mind / Wiring / Limbs).
  3. Stats: Chutzpah +3, Moxie +2, Gumption +1 (set by the Form). She puts Nerve +0, Grit −1 (she's skinny, but steady around live wires).
  4. Origin: Ward Militia: Squad Tactics; +2 on group initiative, Brace as Quick once per combat.
  5. Knacks: Squad Tactics, Electrical Repair, Rooftop Routes.
  6. Augments (6):
    • Mind (Bio): Uplink (Root), Intrude, Commanding Voice.
    • Wiring (Chrome): Quickened (Root), Slipstream.
    • Limbs (Bio): Natural Weapons (Root).

She has both Materials, so she is a Splice. Unlocked: Dread, Link, Shock, Blaze, Haste, Wave, Snare.

  1. Sequence (d4, Prime 2):
#SurgeBuildFluxAt level 1
1Sizzle LineWave + Blaze (30-ft line; Moxie via Wiring)1+3 vs each Guard, 2d6 Blaze, Burning
2BrownoutBolt + Shock (Moxie via Wiring)1+3, 2d8+2 Shock, Dazed
3Dead AirBolt + Dread (Chutzpah via Mind)1+4, 2d8+3 Psychic, Shaken
4Wild

Firmware can swap in Sizzle Line or Brownout (they use Blaze/Shock from her Chrome Wiring); Dead Air uses only Bio Mind parts, so it can't be swapped in.

  1. Gear: Face kit (Concealed Pistol, Light melee, Hack deck, Flashbang, +50 Scrip) + common items. 100 Scrip; buys a Medkit (25), 75 left. Upkeep 25 for Wiring, prepaid for mission 1.
  2. Numbers: Rank 1 · HP 10 · Armor 1 · Speed 40 · Dodge +3, Endure +0, Resist +1 · Flux Limit 4 (4 + 1 + 0 = 5, −1 Splice) · Knit 2 · Juice 1. Attacks: Mind Spike +4, 1d8+3 Psychic (60 ft) · Claws +3, 1d8+2 · Knife +3, 1d6+2 · Pistol +1, 1d6. Material: Knit 2 HP (2 Bio trees × Rank 1); Firmware; Overload rolls both tables; disadvantage vs Shock.
  3. Drive: She took the Mutagen to survive a substation fire. She wants the Ward's grid back on. She owes Scrapjack boss Tallow a new spine.

Playing her at level 1: her Limit of 4 is tiny, so two Surges and a Churn is an Overload. Lead with Dead Air, keep Commanding Voice (Quick Rally, +4 temporary HP to everyone) for the bad round, and stay behind the Juggernaut.

14. Appendix: Arcade vs Tabletop#

The arcade (Gauntlet mode) plays these rules on a battle map, with the computer running the enemies. Almost everything it does is the tabletop rule, read on a grid (Positioning). This appendix lists what it does differently, so nobody mistakes a video-game setting for a rule. When the two disagree, this book wins.

The full audit (every mechanic checked against the engine and the simulators, 2026-10-29) is in Current_Work.md, Rules Audit.

Difficulty Settings (not rules)#

  • Party size is the difficulty. Easy, Medium and Hard field 5, 4 and 3 freelancers.
  • Threat factors. On top of the book's Hard budget, the arcade multiplies minion budgets and Boss HP by ×1.0 / ×1.22 / ×1.38 (Boss damage by half of that), ramping in over levels 1–3. These are tuned so a whole 20-fight run is winnable but not certain. Use the book's budgets at the table (Threats).
  • Mercy. In standard mode a lost fight can be retried from its start; each retry takes 6% off the enemies' HP and 4% off their damage. There's no tabletop equivalent: at the table, a lost fight is a story event (Going Down).
  • GRAFT recovery. In standard mode a freelancer who dies comes back at the next Lockdown with a permanent Scar or Fault. Permadeath mode plays death straight.
  • Fixed rhythm. Every level is a minion fight, a Breather, a Boss (or centrepiece) fight, a level-up and a Lockdown. Minion fights use one or two creature types from one faction (at most 8 creatures); levels without one of the three Bosses use the closest-rated Elite, Brute, Controller, Artillery or Soldier, scaled like a Boss.

Automation (the computer plays a part for you)#

  • Auto-play ("Auto this turn", "Auto: rest of round", "Auto-battle") is a computer player. It is not a rule and it's not optimal.
  • Reactions fire on their own when they help: Bulwark, Threat Sense, Precog (only for big hits), Unbreakable, Reflex Spike, Fortress, Omen, Deadeye, Hair Trigger, Opportunity Strikes. At the table you declare them.
  • Last Gasp fires automatically the first time you would drop to 0 HP each Lockdown. At the table it's your choice.
  • Choices made for you: a Splice's Overload keeps the better of the two tables; Bloom Lore rerolls bad results; Hive Mind gives its extra Prime to the ally with the fewest; Puppet picks its own target; Perfect Expression and Echo take the best Surges; Red Mist attacks the nearest creature; the primary node at level-up is picked automatically.
  • Enemy tactics are a fixed AI (Running the Game lists the same tendencies as GM defaults). If nobody has been hurt for three rounds, the auto-player stops playing safe and walks in, so fights can't stall.

Information#

  • Enemy stats are visible (Guard, TN, HP, attacks, ratings). At the table you learn them with Analyze; in the arcade Analyze still matters for Exposed and Weak Spot.
  • Dice resolve at once, so there's no Juice reroll of a d20. Juice can still set a Sequence die and Shrug a condition.

Simplifications#

  • Initiative is always the Moxie group check (no ambushes or surprise rounds).
  • Haste gives the ally one immediate Action (not Unleash) with advantage, but no Move.
  • Mitosis makes one weapon attack at the end of each of your turns and is destroyed by a failed Dodge (35% of the attacks aimed at you go for it).
  • Scars, Faults and injuries gained in a fight apply from the next fight.
  • Grapple / Shove offer Held or Prone (no push).
  • Not modelled: cover, difficult terrain, elevation, Shaken's "can't move closer", Swarms sharing a square, Spore Cloud's "against attacks from outside" (it just Veils), and these node features: Adaptive, Arc Jump, Wall Run, Many Hands' second grab and Extra Arm's Push. Out-of-combat features (Read the Room, Keen, Uplink's mind-speech, Knacks) have nothing to do in a fight-only game.
  • Every creature fills one square, Huge ones included.

The Simulators Behind the Ratings#

The Boss and Minion Ratings in Threats come from tools/encounter_sim.py, which plays without a map. It abstracts positioning: an enemy Area catches each other freelancer with a fixed chance (30% / 45% / 65% for small / medium / large Areas), 15% of freelancer turns and 10% of enemy actions are spent moving instead of attacking, a Held melee enemy loses half its actions, and Fortress's Area halving is applied half the time. Those are modelling choices for theatre-of-the-mind play, not rules. Checked against the grid (tools/grid_budget.js), the budgets hold on a map except for Heavies, which cost ×1¼ on a grid (Threats §7).
